issues.legal_issue: The rent-control statute governs contractual tenancies and its special eviction procedure displaces the ordinary eviction procedure under general property law; a qualifying subletting after the statutory cutoff may therefore support eviction under the statute.
material_facts: The tenant leased non-residential premises in 1944 and sublet portions in 1957, when neither the lease nor the then-applicable rent-control law prohibited subletting.
The later rent-control statute permitted eviction where, after its stated cutoff, a tenant sublet without the landlord’s written consent and the lease did not confer a right to sublet.
The landlord applied for eviction under that statute, and the court found the 1957 subletting covered by its terms.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control statute applied to the contractual tenancy, and the subletting could support eviction under its special procedure; the ordinary procedure under the Transfer of Property Act did not displace that remedy.
issues.legal_principle: The statute provides a complete code for contractual as well as statutory tenancies, and its special eviction procedure displaces the ordinary eviction procedure under the Transfer of Property Act and an ordinary civil suit. A tenancy remains contractual in origin, but statutory rights and obligations may limit the operation of that contract. Under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, post-cutoff subletting without written consent is a ground for eviction where the lease does not confer a right to sublet. The Court relied on M/s. Raval & Co. v. K. C. Pamachandran and referred to Goppulal v. Thakurji Shriji Dwarkadheeshji.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_sublet_after_statutory_cutoff and subletting_without_written_consent and lease_did_not_grant_subletting_right

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction under a rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_sublet_after_statutory_cutoff: The tenant sublet all or part of the premises after the cutoff specified by the applicable rent-control law.
predicates.subletting_without_written_consent: The tenant sublet without obtaining the landlord’s written consent.
predicates.lease_did_not_grant_subletting_right: The lease did not give the tenant a right to sublet the premises.
predicates.statutory_eviction_remedy_available: The landlord may obtain eviction through the special procedure provided by the rent-control law on the basis of the qualifying subletting.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding under a rent-control law involves post-cutoff subletting without written consent and the lease gives no right to sublet, the statutory eviction remedy is available.

issues.legal_issue: A later amendment removing a former exemption from rent-control coverage is not barred by a savings provision where the eviction proceeding was not brought on the ground of that exemption and the landlord’s ability to seek eviction arose only from the amendment.
material_facts: The premises were a non-residential building that had been exempt from the rent-control statute because of its assessed rental value.
An amendment removed that exemption in 1964.
The landlord commenced the eviction proceeding after the amendment, relying on subletting rather than asserting that the premises were exempt.
The landlord’s ability to use the statutory eviction remedy arose from the removal of the former restriction, rather than from a right previously accrued by virtue of the exemption.
issues.conclusion: The savings provision did not bar the eviction proceeding because it was neither a pending proceeding brought on the ground of exemption nor an enforcement of a landlord’s right accrued by virtue of the former exemption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Amendment Act, 1964, addressed pending proceedings instituted on the ground that a building was exempt under section 30(iii) of the principal Act and rights or privileges accrued to a landlord by virtue of that exemption. The Court held that the proceeding before it fell into neither category: the landlord’s remedy became available through the amendment’s removal of the restriction, not through the former exemption. The amendment’s removal of the restriction enlarged the remedy, and the savings provision could not be read to defeat that change.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction under a rent-control law.
predicates.proceeding_started_after_exemption_remov: The eviction proceeding began after a change removed a former exemption from the rent-control law.
predicates.proceeding_not_brought_on_exemption_grou: The proceeding was not brought on the ground that the premises were exempt from the rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_right_arose_from_removal_of_res: The landlord’s ability to seek the remedy arose because the later change removed a restriction, rather than because the former exemption had granted the landlord a right.
predicates.prior_exemption_savings_do_not_bar_evict: The former exemption’s savings protection does not prevent the eviction proceeding from continuing.

issues.definition: If an eviction proceeding begins after an exemption is removed, is not based on that exemption, and the landlord’s right arises from the removal, the prior-exemption savings protection does not bar the proceeding.
